strategic_network_details:
Gambling Related Harms Community of Improvement for Yorkshire and Humber (Y&H). This is currently led by the Director of Public Health for North Lincolnshire and chaired and coordinated by Shannon Kennedy, Public Health Registrar. The group comprises representatives from all 15 local authorities in the Y&H region. 

The CoI was established around three years ago and to date has developed a framework for action on gambling harms, shared local good practice and supported the design and implementation of a regional programme of work on gambling harms. Funded by a regulatory settlement from the Gambling Commission, this programme of work included the commissioning of training on brief intervention for gambling harms for frontline staff and the commissioning of the Gambling Understood marketing campaign. The CoI is currently coordinating a symposium on gambling harms for local authorities across the north of England and is discussing a strategic approach to spending the forthcoming local authority gambling levy funding, in particular what might be done at a regional level.

priorities_preventing_gambling_harm:
The Sheffield Gambling Harms Prevention Strategy has five strategic priorities as follows:



- Reducing exposure to gambling products, recognising the unfair distribution of gambling harms

- Improving identification and recognition of gambling harms

- Protecting children and young people from gambling industry products and practices

- Influencing the regulatory environment to make prevention a priority

- Providing effective treatment



The strategy's delivery plan features actions under each of these priorities to be implemented by a range of stakeholders. Whilst the strategy sets out what we will do at a local level, it recognises that the most effective policy levers for preventing gambling harms rest at a national level and our Director of Public Health's foreword to the strategy advocates for changes to the Gambling Act.



Locally as a public health service, we are keen to do further work with regulatory services. This includes undertaking test purchasing in local gambling premises (vulnerable persons if possible, age verification if not) and working with colleagues in planning to explore options to prevent the clustering of gambling premises (e.g. development of a supplementary plan) when developing our next Local Plan. To note, staffing capacity in these Council services, and in Public Health, to take forward this work is currently limited.

ph_factors_in_local_area_profile: This document contains the location of allschools, hostels, health services, children’s centres, and hotspots of anti-social behaviour (ASB). This Authority will pay particular attention to applications for the new grant of, or variations to existing, premises licences where those premises lie within areas with a concentration of ASB, hostels/homes for vulnerable people and centres for people with a gambling addiction. The Authority will also pay particular attention to areas where children, young people and families congregate, and areas of high vulnerability and deprivation. This document will be periodically updated and will be publicly available on the Hammersmith and Fulham Council website.
ph_involvement_other_methods: - Through the following requirement: 25.2 Public Health considerations - Although public health is not yet formally a licensing objective there is definitely evidence that problem gamblers and their families are at risk of significant health and social problems such as mental illness, drug and alcohol misuse, relationship breakdown, criminal activity and financial difficulties. The Licensing Authority will liaise with public health colleagues about new and variation applications within the borough, so that we can continue to monitor any increase in access to gambling opportunities for those at risk of problem gambling, check for vulnerable locations nearby eg drug and alcohol clinics or homeless hostels, and work jointly to ensure that appropriate measures are put in place to minimise that risk and support those seeking help.

Currently, activity relating to gambling-related harm within the Public Health team is limited due to capacity and funding constraints; however, we recognise this as an emerging area of need locally.



Our priority is to increase awareness of gambling-related harm across partner agencies and to ensure it is considered alongside wider addictions and mental health support. We aim to strengthen links with treatment providers and national support services, and to improve signposting pathways for residents who may require help.



We also intend to incorporate gambling harm into existing prevention work where possible, including training and awareness for frontline staff, safeguarding discussions, and brief advice within substance misuse and wider wellbeing services.



Developing a more coordinated local approach, informed by national guidance and partnership working (including licensing, community safety and primary care), is a longer-term priority as resources allow.

regional_hna_improvements:
The regional GRH Health Needs Assessment could be improved by comparing our findings with neighbouring Local Authorities that share similar demographics, deprivation levels, and diverse communities to identify best practices and gaps. 

Strengthening the mapping of local referral pathways, expanding engagement with people with lived experience and frontline staff, and improving access to high‑quality, localised data would provide deeper insights into unmet needs. 

Finally, translating these findings into clearer, actionable, and locally tailored recommendations would significantly enhance the value of the HNA for our Local Authority.

It would increase the profile of GRH and promote collaborative working across the region.



It would also support with relevant changes that will take place after LGR.

priorities_preventing_gambling_harm:
Our biggest priorities for preventing gambling related harm in the Local Authority are centered on implementing the recommendations from our comprehensive Gambling Harms Needs Assessment. This includes progressing the key actions within our local action plan and working collaboratively through the Gambling Forum/ relevant steering groups to ensure they are embedded effectively across the system. A core priority is to reduce gambling related harms using a trauma informed, person centred approach that supports residents safely and sensitively. We are focused on raising awareness, reducing stigma, strengthening prevention measures, improving and standardising referral pathways, and building a consistent model of support across all organisations.



In addition, we are prioritising robust aftercare, recognising that ongoing support is essential for sustained recovery (building on the success of the local drug and alcohol recovery partnership) , and ensuring that families and affected others are included in prevention, early intervention, and support pathways. Embedding routine enquiry across services remains a key priority to help residents feel more confident discussing gambling related harms. To support delivery, we have RAG rated the action plan to determine what can be achieved and monitor the outcomes.

Combine OHID prevalence estimates with local service data (IAPT, substance misuse, debt advice, homelessness, police, suicide prevention) to build a robust epidemiological profile and inequality lens.



Establish a standardised core dataset for Kent‑commissioned gambling prevention and VCSE programmes, aligned to the OHID digital data collection solution.



Agree a timetable to embed gambling indicators within the wider JSNA and relevant topic chapters (mental health, substance misuse, suicide prevention, financial hardship).



Formalise a Kent & Medway multi‑agency gambling harms steering group (PH, licensing, mental health, substance misuse, debt, VCSE, lived experience).



Produce a Kent‑specific gambling JSNA section using OHID’s local prevalence data package and small‑area estimates and refresh on a rolling basis.



Develop and adopt a Kent gambling harms action plan, aligned to ADPH Yorkshire & Humber framework and emerging best practice from Yorkshire & Humber and Glasgow.



Co‑design a Kent communications plan using OHID’s nine‑step resource (objective, framing, perceptions, target audience, messaging, reach, delivery, evaluation, tools) and the GM language guide principles.



Use JSNA outputs and local estimates to target communities with higher risk (e.g. areas of deprivation, young adults, people with existing addiction/mental‑health issues).



Build in evaluation from the outset (reach, engagement, help‑seeking, attitudinal change) and share findings with OHID and regional partners.



Work with district licensing teams to develop or enhance Local Area Profiles using OHID small‑area data and local vulnerability indicators, and integrate PH input into licensing committee reports.



Explore local levers to reduce exposure (e.g. conditions on premises, local advertising policies, links to planning) and share learning with CfGS and LGA networks.

​



Include gambling harms in routine licensing training/briefings for councillors, drawing on CfGS case studies.

​

Complete a stocktake of all Kent VCSE organisations currently encountering gambling harms (debt, housing, MH, youth, criminal justice), including any previous industry‑linked funding that needs to be declared.



Co‑design pathways between PH, VCSE, primary care, and specialist gambling treatment (NHS clinics, Southern Gambling Service once expanded) to streamline referral and feedback.



Prepare Kent to act as a local commissioner/partner for VCSE prevention programmes from 2028–29, embedding gambling harms within existing VCSE commissioning frameworks.

​

Establish a small lived‑experience reference group or work with existing regional networks to advise on Kent JSNA, communications and training.



Ensure that all commissioned programmes (training, campaigns, VCSE projects) demonstrate how they address inequalities, including specific work with CYP and affected others.



Embed gambling harms within existing Kent strategies (suicide prevention, mental health, substance misuse, inequalities) and ensure consistent reference in district Gambling Statements of Principles.



Develop a Kent public‑health position on industry relationships and apply the GM‑style training/education assessment tool for all local offers.



Use the OHID menu of interventions to prioritise 2–3 core strands for the first two years (e.g. workforce training, licensing‑linked harm reduction, and targeted community awareness).

A mid-term strategy update was presented to Nottingham City Health and Wellbeing Board in November 2025 - https://committee.nottinghamcity.gov.uk/documents/s176467/Nottingham%20City%20Gambling%20Related%20Harm%20Strategy%202023-2028%20mid-term%20update.pdf 



In summary, the priorities for the remaining lifetime of the strategy are to:

(1)	Evaluate the use of single identification questions in services, including assessing their acceptability and ability to generate referrals to gambling harm support services. 

(2)	We would like to work towards influencing the Council’s sponsorship policy to ensure it considers the potential impact of gambling-related harm, particularly by avoiding partnerships or sponsorships that may promote or normalise gambling among vulnerable groups. 

(3)	We wish to build on the health needs assessment and similar work on an alcohol licensing matrix by gathering data on the licensing of gambling premises across Nottingham and assessing in relation to population need.

(4)	Continue to address inequalities of access, experience and outcomes of gambling support services for people in Nottingham using service data from commissioned services to identify gaps and address potential barriers.

NS Licencing 'Statement of Principles 2025-2027' ask for additional protections above and beyond the requirements of the Gambling Act 2005. Additional requests include:

•	Operators produce a detailed local area risk assessment and mitigation plan that considers nearby vulnerability factors (such as school/colleges, youth centres, homeless hostels, rehabs, mental health services, payday loan or pawn brokers, alcohol premises, fast food outlets, other gambling venues, banks/ATMS, areas of deprivation)

•	NS highlights types of locations where extra scrutiny may apply before a licence is agreed, this includes sites in proximity to schools, youth clubs, leisure centres used by youth, places used by vulnerable people. NS reserves the right to apply extra conditionality if premises are in proximity to the above.

•	NS statement explicitly highlights the need for consideration of deprivation and vulnerable populations. Vulnerable groups include people experiencing mental health problems, unemployed people, people experiencing homelessness, and people living in deprived areas. 

•	NS request that operators complete DBS for staff, have safeguarding policies in place, age verification training, ability to separate gambling areas from areas used by children, and can evidence staff training. 

•	Council will use inspections to monitor these standards

Islington Council, together with the other North Central London councils (Camden, Barnet, Enfield, Haringey) and two VCSE partners (Thrive London and MIND Haringey), have formed the North Central London Tackling Gambling Harms Coalition with £250,000  secured over two years from the Network to Reduce Gambling Harm’s (GREO) Community Investment Programme. hna_research_details:
6 x focus groups with 77 children and young people aged 11-18 in Derby City. We asked the following questions: 

1. Where have you seen gambling advertisements or gambling machines or shops? 

2. Why do young people gamble? 

3. What do you think the potential risks of gambling are? 

4. How does it make you feel when you see gambling ads? 

5. Do different characteristics affect gambling participation (e.g., religion, culture, sex)? 

6. How do you think gambling affects your health and wellbeing? 

7. What do you think would stop you from gambling? 

Focus group data was thematically analysed by 2x staff. Results are available in our DPH report 2023: https://www.derby.gov.uk/health-and-social-care/public-health/documents-publications/#page-2

Regarding the regional HNA, this was last updated in November 2025,. Consequently, the policy information and changes to the funding landscape are particularly useful, and have acted as a reference point for officers working on the GRH agenda. 



Although the assessment provides a handful of local case studies, the OHID Midlands HNA doesn't zoom in on what local authorities can actually do when it comes to implementing interventions to reduce GRH. 



There is a level of ambiguity with the recommendations. One example of this is that that it's suggested that local authorities produce a HNA/strategy but the text doesn't consider the 'so what' and how to apply the HNA to improving population health. Similarly, the regional HNA recommends 'working closely with licensing', but in what capacity and the specific role of public health in the wider ecosystem. Furthermore, the HNA does not consider what activities and measures need to be undertaken to involve experts by lived experience in local work; there lacks a template or a narrative of prior experiences. 



On the other hand, the menu of interventions developed by OHID for local authorities may provide more guidance on some of these intricacies.

strategic_network_details:
Yes, in part: Led by Lancaster University we have recently been involved in a successful funding bid to UKRI's Gambling research and innovation Partnerships to create a new gambling harms network across the North West and then nationally.



The project referred to as Grace-Net (Gambling, Resilience, Awareness & Community Engagement Network) will be the Uk's first dedicated research and innovation network for gambling harm prevention, protection and recovery. The network will act as a regional testbed and national catalyst, linking local expertise to the UKRI gambling harms hub and will produce scalable, evidence-based innovations. 



The project will deliver regional benefits through better data, improved coordination and earlier intervention, while creating a replicable model for use across the UK. 



Alongside ourselves at Lancashire County Council, the project involves Lancaster University, Beacon Counselling Trust, Blackpool Council, Empowerment, Lancashire and South Cumbria Foundation Trust, Liverpool City Council, Liverpool John Moores University, Red Card Gambling, and YGAM.

training_needed:
As an authority, we work closely with Beacon Counselling Trust to deliver the Bet You Can Help training programme. This training applies a first aid style methodology that equips staff to deliver early brief interventions for individuals at risk of, or currently experiencing, gambling related harms, as well as to signpost appropriately to specialist support services. This training is helpful for frontline staff employed by the county council and partner services including those working across Children's Social Care, Adult Social Care, Schools, Primary Care, Drug and Alcohol Treatment etc.



Training should be carefully tailored to the professional groups it targets, ensuring participants gain a strong grounding in knowledge and understanding, along with clarity on how to apply this in practice – beyond those working on the frontline too. There is increasing emphasis on shaping planning and licensing environments to support the prevention and reduction of gambling-related harm. In this context, a comprehensive, evidence informed awareness raising training package for professionals in these areas would be highly valuable in influencing - one that reflects the specific demands and realities of their roles, such as Local Plan development cycles or licensing responsibilities under the Gambling Act. A train the trainer model for Public Health staff could be an effective approach, enabling them to deliver locally tailored sessions within their own teams while building leadership and capacity across the system. 



Given the evolving national landscape surrounding gambling and gambling related harm, OHID-led training or webinars on emerging national developments would also be valuable. This would not need to be frequent, but timely updates in response to significant legislative, policy, or sector changes would help ensure local authorities remain aligned and well informed.



Finally, the availability and interpretation of national data on gambling participation and gambling harms remains limited. Additional training to support understanding of national data sources, such as those provided by the Gambling Commission and how these can be applied to local needs assessment and targeted intervention planning would strengthen our ability to tailor support to priority populations, including communities experiencing higher levels of deprivation.
training_commissioned_other_workforces:
Beacon Counselling Trust's Bet you can Help Now training was delivered to the Lancashire Safeguarding Partnership - a statutory, multi-agency collaborative, comprising local authorities, police, and NHS Integrated Care Boards. The LSP is responsible for ensuring effective safeguarding for children and adults across Lancashire, Blackpool, and Blackburn with Darwen.

 

In addition, training has been rolled out across our Public Health workforce, including those colleagues working specifically on workstreams relating to Mental Health, Drugs and Alcohol.



Although not delivered as formal training, Beacon Counselling Trust attended a Household Support Fund Working Group, which included representatives from all 12 district councils. Their input followed queries about how to financially support residents who were engaged in gambling activity. The session helped build foundational awareness of gambling-related harm, offered guidance on communicating in a non stigmatising way with those affected, and highlighted relevant local support services available for signposting.

campaign_target_audiences:
Utilising levy funding, we are preparing to deliver a Lancashire wide summer communications campaign focused on raising awareness of gambling related harms. The campaign is scheduled to run during a peak period in the sporting calendar, including major events such as the FIFA World Cup, to maximise visibility and relevance.



The campaign will be developed in collaboration with individuals with lived experience of gambling related harms, supported by our partners at Beacon Counselling Trust and colleagues across Blackpool and Blackburn with Darwen Councils. We also intend to draw on insights and effective messaging from recent campaigns led by GambleAware, Chapter One, and Liverpool City Council. This approach will help ensure that the campaign is both evidence informed and impactful.



In terms of target audiences, our approach is guided by national evidence on groups at heightened risk of gambling related harm. Key demographic and socioeconomic groups include males, adults aged 16–34, individuals with limiting long term physical health conditions, those experiencing poor mental health or mental illness, and people with a higher prevalence of substance misuse. These groups will form the primary focus of our campaign activity. We have also reviewed PGSI data to identify those districts in Lancashire with a greater prevalence of severity, to be able to target comms activity more effectively.

priorities_preventing_gambling_harm:
At Lancashire County Council, our main priorities for preventing gambling‑related harm are set out within our Public Health Framework for Action on Gambling Harms – based on the 'Public Health Framework for Preventing and Reducing Gambling Harms in Yorkshire and the Humber' - which outlines our strategic approach:

•	Build and share the evidence base on gambling harms - using data and insight to inform targeted action. This includes collaborating with academic partners, working alongside people with lived experience to shape decision‑making, and undertaking a comprehensive Health Needs Assessment to understand the prevalence, distribution, inequalities and types of harm experienced across Lancashire.

•	Reducing exposure and access - developing a local evidence base to inform public health recommendations to influence the regulatory environment. This includes feeding into planning policy, contributing to district councils’ Statements of Licensing Policy, and reviewing the use of local authority‑owned or managed advertising space for gambling products, including considering restrictions where appropriate.

•	Raising awareness and building understanding of gambling‑related harms - this will be achieved through various countywide communication campaigns on risk and harm, reviewing gambling‑harms education and training within settings attended by children and young people, and developing, offering and promoting evidence‑based training to frontline staff and partners. Internally, we are working to sign the Beacon Counselling Trust Workplace Charter, deliver workforce campaigns, review training gaps, and raise awareness among elected members.

•	Treatment and support - with a focus on increasing visibility and accessibility of support services. This also includes improving identification and signposting across varying sectors including health, social care and wider VCFSE, strengthening workplace health support across Lancashire-based organisations/businesses.

•	Building leadership and capability - involves contributing to national consultations, actively participating in regional and national networks, and reviewing the opportunity to develop a cross‑council strategy aligned with the Lancashire Suicide and Self‑Harm Prevention Strategy to create a coordinated systemwide approach.

The consultation response set out Tower Hamlets Public Health’s position on the Draft Gambling Licensing Policy 2025–2028, explaining why gambling is a significant public‑health issue, how local factors such as deprivation, mental‑health need, substance misuse, unemployment, and the clustering of 54 betting shops increase vulnerability to harm, and why Public Health supported the overall direction of the draft policy. priorities_preventing_gambling_harm:
1. Advocate - 

Advocating for a fairer and healthier gambling system using strong governance, robust evidence, and cross‑sector partnerships to reduce exposure to harmful gambling products and the prevalence of gambling at risky or harmful levels in Southampton. Promotion and sharing of learning from the Scrutiny Inquiry to influence gambling legislative reform locally, regionally and nationally to reduce gambling products. 





2. Network -

Make connections and establish partnerships across an array of local stakeholders to enable a collaborative approach to prevent gambling at harmful levels and harmful gambling products across the local region.  





3. Communicate - 

Strengthening communication through coordinated campaigns, consistent harm‑aware language, and strong partnerships that keep harmful gambling visible and openly discussed. Collaboration with key stakeholders and partners on public‑facing campaigns, and working with schools, parents and youth settings to deliver specialist‑led, evidence‑based gambling-related harms awareness sessions for children and young people. All of which would be underpinned by continuous learning from people with lived experience. 





4. Educate - 

Educate residents by sharing clear, evidence‑informed messages about gambling harms, grounded in the Southampton Gambling-related harms Health Needs Assessment and strengthened through collaboration with academic partners. Prioritize training for elected members, leaders and frontline workers which would benefit residents, staff and partners to make informed decisions about gambling for their health and wellbeing.

Appendix 5 – Public Health Information  

Gambling harms are the impacts from gambling that can affect the health and wellbeing of 

individuals, communities and wider society, and are a key public health concern. The harms 

from gambling are diverse and can impact not only an individual but also associated social 

networks (such as family and friends, known as ‘Affected Others’). Anyone can be harmed by 

gambling, however harms are not evenly distributed. 

For each person who experiences gambling harm around six other individuals are affected, 

often partners and children. Women are more likely to experience this type of harm and 

severity increases according to closeness of relationship with the person gambling at elevated 

risk levels. 

The harms from gambling are varied, and may also be interconnected. Harms include (but are 

not limited to): Increased stress and impacts on mental health and wellbeing (such as anxiety, 

depression and suicide risk) Relationship breakdown Domestic abuse Financial hardship. The 

bottom line is that everyone who gambles is at risk of addiction and is at risk of experiencing 

harms related to gambling. (Greater Manchester Combined Authority, Association of Directors 

of Public Health (ADPH) Yorkshire and Humber and ADPH North East) 2024 

For further information on gambling harms visit the NHS webpage on gambling addiction at: 

https://www.nhs.uk/live-well/addiction-support/gambling-addiction/

The 2005 Gambling Act sets out how gambling in Great Britain is regulated. In the act, 

gambling is defined as playing a game of chance for a prize, betting and participating in a 

lottery. 

In recent years, concern about the harms associated with gambling has been increasing and 

in March 2018, the Public Health England (PHE) remit letter confirming PHE’s priorities for 

2018 to 2019 included the request for PHE to ‘inform and support action on gambling-related 

harm as part of the follow up to the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport-led review 

of gaming machines and social responsibility’. 

In May 2018, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport published its response to 

a consultation on proposals for changes to gaming machines and social responsibility 

measures. In it they announced that ‘PHE will conduct an evidence review of the health 

aspects of gambling-related harm to inform action on prevention and treatment’. 

The UK has one of the biggest gambling markets in the world, generating a profit of £14.2 

billion in 2020. Previous research has shown that harms associated with gambling are wide

priorities_preventing_gambling_harm:
•	Strengthen early identification - Improve the ability of services and partners to recognise gambling related harm at the earliest opportunity.

•	Increase awareness across communities and services - Deliver consistent messaging and campaigns to improve public understanding of harms and where to seek support.

•	Ensure accessible and safe support pathways- Improve referral routes between frontline services and specialist support to make help easier to access.

•	Reduce stigma - Promote non judgemental, sensitive approaches that encourage individuals and communities to seek help without fear.

•	Target support to higher risk communities -Focus prevention activity on groups with greater vulnerability, including those experiencing inequalities.

•	Embed gambling harm prevention across wider system priorities -Integrate gambling harm work with mental health, suicide prevention, drug and alcohol services, and the inequalities agenda.

•	Align with the GM vision for a gambling harm free region - Contribute to GM wide campaigns and system leadership through the GM Gambling Harms Board.

•	Strengthen licensing, advertising and sponsorship policies - Develop and implement approaches that reduce population exposure to harmful products and practices.

•	Build a skilled and confident workforce - Expand training across the system, including the continued rollout of Chapter One training, to equip staff to identify and respond to gambling related harm.
